topics.title: Two pointers
topics.subtitle: Shrink the search space with every move.
topics.summary: Use two positions to inspect a sequence from opposite ends or around a fixed value. A sorted order often tells you which side to move.
principles: Start at opposite ends when the data is sorted or symmetric.
Use the comparison to discard a whole range of candidates.
Move one pointer at a time and state why the move is safe.

frames.caption: Start with the widest pair. Their sum is 17, which is too large.
frames.state: sum > target → move the right pointer

frames.caption: The sum is 13. It is still too large, so move right inward again.
frames.state: sum > target → move the right pointer

frames.caption: The sum is 9. The target pair is found.

questions.title: Two Sum II — Input Array Is Sorted
questions.prompt: Find two numbers in a sorted array that add to the target.
questions.why: When the sum is too large, moving the right pointer left is the only move that can lower it. When too small, move left rightward.

frames.caption: 2 + 15 = 17. Too large; move right left.
2 + 11 = 13. Still too large; keep moving right left.
2 + 7 = 9. Return the 1-indexed positions.

steps: Start at Python indices 0 and 3. Their values sum to 17, so move the right pointer left.
At indices 0 and 2 the sum is 13. Move the right pointer left again.
Now 2 + 7 = 9. Convert indices 0 and 1 to the requested positions 1 and 2.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: Each move discards an endpoint that cannot form the target with any remaining value.
walkthrough.cost: O(n) time because either pointer moves at most n positions in total. O(1) extra space.
walkthrough.pitfall: Use the sort order already provided and return 1-based positions.

questions.title: Container With Most Water
questions.prompt: Choose two lines that hold the most water.
questions.why: The shorter wall limits the water height. Moving the taller wall inward only reduces width without improving the limiting height, so move the shorter wall.

frames.caption: Area = min(1, 7) × 8 = 8. The left wall is shorter, so advance the left pointer one position to the right.
Area = min(8, 7) × 7 = 49. The right wall is shorter, so move the right pointer one position to the left.
Area = min(8, 3) × 6 = 18. Width shrinks; the best remains 49.

steps: At the ends, the width is 8 and the shorter wall has height 1. The area is 8 × 1 = 8.
Move past height 1. Now the walls at indices 1 and 8 have width 7 and shorter height 7. Record area 49.
Move the right pointer this time because height 7 is shorter. Keep computing areas and stop when the pointers meet. The best stays 49.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: Keeping the shorter wall and moving the other inward cannot improve the current area because width decreases and the height is still capped by that shorter wall.
walkthrough.cost: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
walkthrough.pitfall: Use the smaller wall height and the distance between indices. Sorting the input would change those distances.

questions.title: 3Sum
questions.prompt: Find unique triplets whose sum is zero.
questions.why: Sort first. Fix one value, then use two pointers on the remaining sorted suffix; skip equal values to avoid duplicate triplets.

frames.caption: Fix −4. The sum is −3, so move left to increase it.
The sum is still negative. Move left past the duplicate −1.
Fix −1. The triplet [−1, −1, 2] sums to zero.
Move both pointers inward after the first match. The second match uses 0 and 1. Both triplets are distinct.

steps: Sort to [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]. Fix -4 and search the suffix for a pair totaling 4. Even the two largest values sum to 3, so there is no match.
Fix the first -1. The next -1 and last 2 sum to 1, giving [-1, -1, 2]. Move both pointers inward.
The values 0 and 1 also sum to 1. Record [-1, 0, 1]. Skip the next fixed -1 because it would repeat work.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: Fixing one value reduces the task to finding all pairs with a known sum in a sorted suffix.
walkthrough.cost: O(n²) time. The pointer scan uses O(1) extra space beyond results, plus any memory used by the sort.
walkthrough.pitfall: Skip duplicate values at the same role after a match. Equal values can still be valid at two different positions.

lesson.intuition: A pointer here is just a number that tells you which position to look at. Imagine a sorted row of cards. To make a target sum, start with the first and last card. If the sum is too big, the last card cannot pair with any card still in the row because the first card is already the smallest. Cross off the last card and try again.

terms.definition: A position in the list. Python starts counting at zero.
Reading left to right, values stay the same or increase.
The part of the list that still might contain the answer.

steps: Put one pointer at each end of the sorted list.
Add the values at the pointers. If the sum matches, return those positions.
If the sum is too small, move the left pointer one step right. If it is too large, move the right pointer one step left.
Stop when the two pointers meet. A pair must use two different positions.

check.question: With [2, 7, 11, 15] and target 13, which pointer moves first?
check.answer: Move the right pointer left. Even the smallest available value, 2, makes 15 too large. The next pair is 2 + 11 = 13.

topics.title: Sliding window
topics.subtitle: Grow a valid range, then shrink it when needed.
topics.summary: Keep a moving interval over a string or array. Expand the right edge to include new data, then move the left edge to restore the rule or improve the answer.
principles: Track what the current window contains.
Move the right edge to explore new input.
Move the left edge only when the window condition requires it.

frames.caption: The window “abc” has no repeats. Record length 3.
The next “a” repeats. Move left past the previous a; the new window is “bca”.
Keep expanding and shrinking while preserving a duplicate-free window.

questions.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
questions.prompt: Find the longest substring with no repeated characters.
questions.why: A map of last-seen positions lets the left edge jump past a duplicate while never moving backwards.

frames.caption: “abc” is valid and has length 3.
The second a repeats. Move left just past its old position.
The second b repeats. Move left past the old b; never move it backwards.

steps: Read a, b, and c. All are different, so the best length is 3.
At the second a, its last position is 0. Set left to 1 so the window becomes bca.
Apply the same rule for each later duplicate. A duplicate outside the current window cannot push left backwards.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: A duplicate inside the window forces the start past the previous copy. Keeping the earliest valid start gives the longest window for this end position.
walkthrough.cost: O(n) time with a dictionary of last positions and O(u) space for u distinct characters.
walkthrough.pitfall: Use left = max(left, last_seen[char] + 1) when you have seen the character before.

questions.title: Minimum Window Substring
questions.prompt: Find the shortest substring that contains every required character, including duplicates.
questions.why: Expand until all required counts are met. Then shrink from the left while the window remains valid, saving the shortest valid range.

frames.caption: The range ADOBEC contains A, B, and C. The window is valid.
Removing A makes the window invalid. Expand right to find A again.
BANC contains every required letter and is the shortest range found.

steps: Read until the first C. ADOBEC now covers A, B, and C. Save it before moving left past A.
Expand again until a later A restores coverage. Remove surplus letters and save each shorter valid window.
At the final C, shrink past the leading surplus letters until the window is BANC. Removing B now breaks coverage.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: For each right edge, shrinking while all required letter counts still hold finds the shortest valid window ending there.
walkthrough.cost: O(|s| + |t|) time because each edge advances at most |s| times. O(u) space for counts of the u letters required by t.
walkthrough.pitfall: Count repeated requirements. For t = "AAB", one A and one B is insufficient.

questions.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
questions.prompt: Find the longest substring that can be made of one repeated character with at most k replacements.
questions.why: A window is valid when its length minus the most frequent character count is at most k.

frames.caption: AABA has one non-A character, so one replacement makes four As.
AABAB needs two replacements, exceeding k = 1. Move left forward.
After one removal, ABAB has two As and two Bs. It still needs two replacements, so move left again.
BAB contains two Bs and one A. It is valid again. The best length seen remains 4.
Extend to BABB. Change the single A to B to get another valid window of length 4.

steps: In AABA, there are three As. Change the single B to A, making a run of length 4.
Extending to AABAB requires two replacements, because the most common letter occurs three times out of five. Trim from the left until the window is valid.
Keep extending and trimming. Another valid length-four window is BABB after changing A to B.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: Keeping the most common letter minimizes replacements, so the number to change is window length minus its frequency.
walkthrough.cost: Scanning 26 uppercase letter counts to get the true maximum is O(26n) = O(n) time and O(26) space.
walkthrough.pitfall: Check the count of the most common letter inside the current window. The most common letter across the whole input can differ.

lesson.intuition: Think of a sliding window as a highlight over neighboring characters. The right edge includes one new character at a time. When the highlight breaks a rule, move its left edge until the rule is satisfied again. Keep counts or positions so you can update the highlight without reading all of it again.

terms.definition: Every element between the first and last positions is included.
The current range from left to right, inclusive. Its length is right − left + 1.
The current window satisfies the problem’s rule, such as having no repeated letters.

steps: Write the rule in one sentence. For example, “each letter appears at most once.”
Move the right edge to include one new character and update its count.
For a longest valid window, move left until the rule holds, then record the length. For a shortest covering window, keep shrinking while the coverage still holds.
Save the best length or range seen across all right positions.

check.question: You have the window abc, then the next character is a. What is the smallest change that restores validity?
check.answer: Remove the earlier a. The window becomes bca. The later a remains in the window.

topics.title: Hash maps
topics.subtitle: Trade a little memory for fast lookups.
topics.summary: Record values or counts as you scan. A hash map can answer “have I seen this?” or “how often?” without repeatedly searching the whole input.
principles: Choose a key that captures the property you need.
Update the map as each value is processed.
Be clear about whether your map stores indices, counts, or groups.

frames.caption: Before storing 2, compute the complement needed for target 9.
At 7, the map already contains its complement 2.
Store the value and index only after checking, so one item cannot match itself.

questions.title: Two Sum
questions.prompt: Return the indices of two values that add to the target.
questions.why: For each value, look up its complement among values already seen. This avoids checking every pair.

frames.caption: At 2, the complement is 7. It is not in the map, so store 2 → index 0.
At 7, the complement is 2. The map finds it immediately.

steps: For 2, look up the number needed to reach 9, which is 7. The dictionary is empty, so store 2 at index 0.
For 7, the number needed is 2. The dictionary already holds index 0.
Return index 0 and your current index 1.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: Every pair has a later index. When the scan reaches it, the earlier number is already in the dictionary.
walkthrough.cost: O(n) expected time and O(n) extra space.
walkthrough.pitfall: Look up the needed number before inserting the current one so the two positions are distinct.

questions.title: Group Anagrams
questions.prompt: Group words that contain the same letters in a different order.
questions.why: Map each word to a canonical key, such as its sorted letters, then append the word to that key’s bucket.

frames.caption: “eat” becomes the canonical key “aet”. Create that bucket.
“tea” and “ate” produce the same key, so they join the bucket.
“tan” and “nat” share key “ant”; “bat” starts another group.

steps: Sort the characters of eat to get the key aet. Start a list under that key.
tea and ate produce the same key, so append both original words to the same list.
tan and nat produce ant. bat produces abt. Return the dictionary’s lists.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: Two words with exactly the same letters and counts produce the same sorted string.
walkthrough.cost: For n words of length at most k, O(nk log k) time and O(nk) space including stored keys and groups.
walkthrough.pitfall: Keep duplicate letters in the key. A set of characters would group ab and aab together incorrectly.

questions.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
questions.prompt: Return the length of the longest consecutive-value sequence in an unsorted array.
questions.why: Put values in a set and start counting only at numbers whose predecessor is absent. Each run is then scanned once.

frames.caption: 4 has predecessor 3, so it is not the start of a run.
1 has no predecessor. Count 1, 2, 3, 4.
200 starts a run of length 1. The longest run remains four.

steps: Build a set of the numbers. When you inspect 4, notice that 3 exists, so 4 cannot start a run.
At 1, check 0. It is absent, so 1 starts a run. Look up 2, 3, 4, and stop at missing 5.
Other starts such as 100 and 200 each give length 1. The best length is 4.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: Only the smallest member of each run lacks a predecessor. Starting there means the successful forward lookups across all runs visit each distinct number once.
walkthrough.cost: O(n) expected time and O(n) extra space.
walkthrough.pitfall: Iterate the set itself so repeated copies of a run’s starting value do not make you count that run again.

lesson.intuition: A Python dictionary is like an index in the back of a book. Give it a key and it quickly retrieves the associated value. While scanning an array you can record answers to questions you will need later, such as where a number first appeared or how many times you have seen it.

terms.definition: The thing you look up, such as a number or a normalized word.
The information stored for that key, such as an index, a count, or a list of words.
A collection used to ask whether a key exists when no associated value is needed.

steps: Decide what repeated lookup is slowing down the simple solution.
Choose a key that lets you answer that lookup directly.
Choose the value you need to keep. Use a set when presence alone is enough.
Scan the input and check whether to look up before updating. For matching two positions, looking up first avoids matching a value with itself.

check.question: For nums = [3, 3] and target = 6, why should you look up 3 before recording the current index?
check.answer: The first 3 sees no earlier 3. The second 3 retrieves index 0, so the returned indices are 0 and 1.

topics.title: Binary search
topics.subtitle: Use the order of a list to rule out about half the positions at each step.
topics.summary: Binary search checks the middle of a range of possible positions. In a sorted list, the middle value tells you which half can still contain the target. Repeat on the remaining range until you find the value or run out of positions.
principles: Before each check, the answer, if present, is still between left and right. This promise is called an invariant.
For an exact match, an inclusive range may contain one item when left equals right. Keep going until left is greater than right.
In a rotated list, first identify a part that is still sorted. Its endpoints tell you whether the target can be in that part.
In a minimum search, keep mid if it could itself be the answer. Every update must make the range smaller.

frames.caption: Look for 9. The possible positions are 0 through 5. The midpoint is index 2, and its value is 3.
Drop indices 0 through 2 because their values are all at most 3. The new midpoint is index 4.
The value at index 4 is 9. Return that position.

questions.title: Binary Search
questions.prompt: Find the index of a target in a sorted array, or return −1.
questions.why: Each midpoint comparison removes half the remaining candidates, giving logarithmic search time.

frames.caption: Look for 9. The possible positions are 0 through 5. The midpoint is index 2, and its value is 3.
Drop indices 0 through 2 because their values are all at most 3. The new midpoint is index 4.
The value at index 4 is 9. Return that position.

steps: Start with left = 0 and right = 5. The middle index (0 + 5) // 2 is 2, and nums[2] is 3.
Because 3 < 9, drop index 2 and everything to its left. The next range is indices 3 through 5.
The new middle index is 4. Its value is 9, so return 4. If the range ever becomes empty instead, return −1.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: Sorted order guarantees that a comparison rules out one side. Since you keep every position where the target could still be, a later check finds it if it exists.
walkthrough.cost: O(log n) checks because each discards about half the remaining positions. O(1) extra space with a loop.
walkthrough.pitfall: When the midpoint cannot match, move past it using mid + 1 or mid − 1. Leaving the same candidate range can make a loop run forever.

questions.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.prompt: Search a rotated sorted array in O(log n) time.
questions.why: At least one half around the midpoint is sorted. Check whether the target lies in that half before discarding the other.

frames.caption: Look for 0. The middle value is 7. The left segment [4, 5, 6, 7] is sorted because it has no drop.
The middle value is 1. The sorted left segment is now [0, 1]. The target 0 could be there, and mid has already failed.
One candidate remains at index 4. Its value is 0, so return the index.

steps: Start at indices 0 and 6. The middle value 7 differs from the target. Since nums[left] ≤ nums[mid], the segment from 4 to 7 is sorted.
The target 0 falls outside 4 through 7, so discard that sorted side and set left = 4.
The next middle value is 1. The sorted left side is [0, 1]. The target is inside its value range, so keep the part before mid and set right = 4.
Check the one remaining position. Index 4 contains 0.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: The rotated input with distinct values has at most one drop. If the left side is sorted, keep it only when nums[left] ≤ target < nums[mid]. Otherwise the right side is sorted and you can use nums[mid] < target ≤ nums[right] to decide whether to keep it. These strict midpoint comparisons apply after checking equality.
walkthrough.cost: O(log n) time because each step keeps just one half. O(1) extra space.
walkthrough.pitfall: Do not discard a half just because the midpoint is greater than the target. The drop in a rotated array can move smaller numbers to the right.

questions.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
questions.prompt: Find the smallest value in a rotated sorted array with unique values.
questions.why: Compare the midpoint to the right edge. That tells you which side still contains the rotation pivot.

frames.caption: The middle value 7 is larger than the rightmost value 2. The drop to the minimum must be after index 3.
The middle value 1 is smaller than the rightmost value 2. From mid to right the values increase, so the minimum can be at mid or to its left.
The new midpoint is index 4. Value 0 is less than value 1 at the right edge, so keep index 4 and move right there.
The range has one element. Return the value at that index.

steps: Compare middle value 7 with the right edge 2. Since 7 > 2, the drop to the smallest element must be after mid. Move left to index 4.
In [0, 1, 2], compare midpoint 1 with rightmost 2. The minimum can be at mid or to its left, so set right = 5 and keep mid.
Now the range is [0, 1]. A comparison of 0 with 1 moves right to 4. The bounds meet and nums[4] is 0.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: When nums[mid] > nums[right], the low part of the rotation is to the right of mid. When nums[mid] < nums[right], the right segment increases, so no position to the right of mid beats mid itself.
walkthrough.cost: O(log n) time and O(1) extra space. Distinct values make each comparison decisive.
walkthrough.pitfall: Use a loop that stops when left equals right. On the smaller-than branch set right = mid because the middle value could be the minimum.

lesson.intuition: Imagine finding room 9 along a hallway where room numbers increase from left to right. If the middle room is 3, room 9 cannot be to its left. You can ignore that entire part of the hallway. The same idea works with a sorted Python list, where each check tells you which positions you can stop considering.

terms.definition: A position in the list. The first index is 0.
The positions still worth checking. In this lesson, left and right both belong to the range.
The middle index, computed as (left + right) // 2. Python’s // rounds down.
A sorted list cut once and rejoined with the back part first. For example, [0, 1, 2, 4] can become [2, 4, 0, 1].

steps: Set left to 0 and right to the last index. If left is greater than right, the range is empty.
Compute mid and compare nums[mid] to the target. If they are equal, return mid.
If the middle value is too small, every index up to mid is too small. Set left = mid + 1. If the middle value is too large, set right = mid − 1.
Repeat on the smaller range. If it becomes empty, return −1. Checking about half as many positions each time gives O(log n) time.

check.question: Search for 2 in [−1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12]. After checking 3 at index 2, which positions remain? What should the search return?
check.answer: Only indices 0 and 1 remain because 3 and everything after it are greater than 2. You next check −1 and then 0. Both are too small, so left advances past right and the result is −1.

topics.title: Prefix sums
topics.subtitle: Save running totals so you can find the sum between two positions.
topics.summary: A prefix total tells you how much you have added before a boundary in a list. Save one total per boundary, then subtract the total before the range from the total after it. The same idea helps count ranges with a target sum.
principles: Use n + 1 boundaries for n numbers. Start with prefix[0] = 0 so ranges beginning at index 0 work too.
With prefix[i] defined as the total before index i, the sum from left through right is prefix[right + 1] − prefix[left].
To count ranges summing to k, look for earlier prefix totals equal to current total − k. Store their counts, including duplicates.
Two running products can cover everything except the current item. Multiplying both sides works even when the input contains zeros.

frames.caption: Boundary 0 comes before the first number. No items have been added, so store 0.
Add 3 and save that total. Then add 1 and save 4.
Add 4 and then 2. Each entry records a total at a different boundary.
For indices 1 through 3, start with the total after index 3 and remove the total before index 1.

questions.title: Range Sum Query — Immutable
questions.prompt: Compute many inclusive range sums for an array whose values stay fixed.
questions.why: Precompute prefix totals once, then answer each query with one subtraction.

frames.caption: Initialize the total before the first item to 0.
Store the total after 2, then add −3. A running total can go down.
Continue with 5 and 1. Keep the completed array for every query.
Query indices 1 through 2. Remove the total before index 1 from the total after index 2.
A second query can reuse the same array without scanning the numbers again.

steps: Start at zero and add each value. Save prefix = [0, 2, −1, 4, 5].
For [1, 2], take prefix[3] = 4. Subtract prefix[1] = 2 to remove the first item. The result is 2.
For [0, 3], subtract the empty total prefix[0] from prefix[4]. The result is 5.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: The larger prefix includes the range plus everything before it. The subtraction cancels the shared earlier items, even when some are negative.
walkthrough.cost: O(n) setup time and O(n) space to store the totals. Each query takes O(1) time.
walkthrough.pitfall: Use right + 1 for the end boundary. On a one-item range [i, i], using prefix[i] twice would return zero.

questions.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
questions.prompt: Count contiguous ranges whose sum is k.
questions.why: The sum from an earlier boundary to the current boundary is the difference of their prefix totals. Count how many earlier boundaries have the required total, then record the current boundary.

frames.caption: Target k is 2. Before any numbers, there is one boundary with total 0.
Add 1. No earlier boundary has total 1 − 2 = −1. Record total 1.
Add −1. The total returns to 0. Record a second boundary with total 0.
Add 2. Two earlier boundaries have total 0, so two ranges ending here have sum 2.
Add 0. The same two starting boundaries make two more ranges with this new ending position.

steps: Begin with seen = {0: 1}. That 0 marks the boundary before the list.
Reading 1 and −1 gives running totals of 1 and 0. Both lookups find no match yet. There are now two recorded boundaries with total 0.
Reading 2 brings the total to 2. Add seen[2 − 2] = 2 to the answer, then record total 2.
Reading 0 leaves the total at 2. The same two starting boundaries pair with this new ending position, giving four ranges in total.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: A range with total k ends at a prefix total that is exactly k more than its starting prefix. Each occurrence of that starting total gives a different range. Negative numbers can make running totals fall, so the count does not rely on sorted totals.
walkthrough.cost: O(n) expected time with a dictionary and O(n) extra space. There are at most n + 1 distinct prefix totals.
walkthrough.pitfall: Look up the needed total before recording the current one. With k = 0, recording it first would count an empty range.

questions.title: Product of Array Except Self
questions.prompt: For each index, multiply all the other numbers in linear time without division.
questions.why: The numbers before and after an index form two disjoint parts. Multiply their products to get the answer for that index.

frames.caption: Sweep left to right and save the product of values before each index. Once you pass the zero, that running product stays zero.
Start the right-to-left sweep with right product 1. Multiply output[3] by 1, then include −1 in the right product.
At index 2, multiply the stored 0 by −1. Then include 3 for the next position.
At the zero, multiply the saved left product 2 by the right product −3 before including the zero.
At index 0, the right side includes the zero. Multiply its saved left product 1 by 0.

steps: Save each left product in the output before multiplying the running total by the current value. Start with 1, so the saved products are [1, 2, 0, 0].
Go right to left with right product starting at 1. At each index multiply the saved left product by the right product, then include this index’s value in the right product.
At index 1, the left product is 2 and the right product is 3 × −1 = −3. That position gives −6. Every other output includes the zero.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: Each position combines all numbers strictly before and strictly after it. The two sides contain every required value exactly once. An empty side has product 1, which leaves the other side unchanged.
walkthrough.cost: O(n) time for two passes and O(1) extra space apart from the required output array.
walkthrough.pitfall: Update the running product after using it for the current index. Updating it first includes the value you need to skip.

lesson.intuition: Imagine a receipt that shows a running total after each purchase. To find what you spent on the last few items, subtract the total printed just before those items from the final total. A prefix sum works the same way for a list of numbers, including negative numbers.

terms.definition: The first part of the list, starting at index 0. The empty prefix contains no items.
A position between numbers. Boundary i is just before index i, so prefix[i] contains the first i numbers.
A part of the list that includes both endpoint indices. The range [1, 3] contains indices 1, 2, and 3.
The last part of the list. In the product example, the right-hand suffix starts just after the index you are skipping.

steps: Make an array of running totals. Start with 0 before the first item.
For each number, add it to the previous total and save the new total. For [3, 1, 4, 2], this gives [0, 3, 4, 8, 10].
To find the sum at indices 1 through 3, take prefix[4] = 10. It includes every item up to and including index 3.
Subtract prefix[1] = 3 to remove the item before the range. The answer is 7.

check.question: With [3, 1, 4, 2], which two prefix entries give the sum at index 2 alone?
check.answer: Use prefix[3] = 8 and prefix[2] = 4. The subtraction 8 − 4 leaves just the number at index 2, which is 4.

principles: Push unresolved items with the information needed later.
Pop only when the current item satisfies the stack condition.
Each item should enter and leave at most once.

questions.why: Build prefix sums P and maintain indices with strictly increasing prefix values. For current j, pop front indices while P[j]−P[front]≥k, updating length j−front. Pop back indices while P[j]≤P[back]: the newer prefix is at least as good for every future endpoint and yields a shorter interval.

frames.caption: For nums=[2,−1,2] and k=3, the displayed values are prefix sums P=[0,2,1,3], not the original array.
Prefix index 1 has value 2; retain it after the initial zero.
Prefix value 1 at index 2 dominates value 2 at index 1. It is smaller and later.
At prefix index 3, P[3]−P[0]=3. Record length 3 and remove front 0; the next difference is only 2.

topics.title: KMP and the prefix function
topics.subtitle: Reuse matched prefixes instead of restarting after a mismatch.
topics.summary: The prefix table pi[i] records the length of the longest proper prefix of s[:i+1] that is also its suffix. When a new character mismatches, fall back from length j to pi[j−1] until a shorter border can extend. KMP uses this table to search text without moving the text pointer backward, taking O(n+m) time for text length n and pattern length m.
principles: A proper prefix excludes the entire string; prefix and suffix occurrences are allowed to overlap.
Build pi left to right: start j=pi[i−1]; while j>0 and s[i]!=s[j], set j=pi[j−1]; increment j on a match, then assign pi[i]=j.
During search, j is the length of the pattern prefix matching the text suffix read so far. On mismatch, follow prefix-table links before comparing the same text character again.
When j equals the pattern length, the match starts at i−m+1. To find overlapping matches, continue with j=pi[m−1].
Each successful extension increases j by one and each fallback decreases it, giving linear total work. The pattern table uses O(m) extra space.

frames.caption: Build pi for ababaca. Through index 4, the longest border is aba, length 3.
At i=5, c does not match s[3]=b. Fall back using pi[2]=1.
c also mismatches s[1]=b, so fall back to pi[0]=0. It mismatches a too.
At i=6, a extends the length-zero border by one.
Every fallback uses a previously proven border; no prefix needs to be rescanned from scratch.

questions.title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
questions.prompt: Return the first position of needle inside haystack, or −1 if no occurrence exists.
questions.why: Build the prefix table for needle and scan haystack with one matched-length pointer. A mismatch changes only that pointer through failure links; the text position never retreats.

frames.caption: Search needle=ababac in haystack=abababac. After text index 4, five pattern characters match.
Text index 5 is b but needle[5] is c. Fall back to pi[4]=3, then match that same b against needle[3].
The next a matches needle[4].
The final c completes all six pattern characters.

questions.title: Repeated Substring Pattern
questions.prompt: Decide whether the string consists of two or more copies of a shorter substring.
questions.why: Let L=pi[n−1] and candidate period p=n−L. Repetition exists exactly when L>0 and n%p==0. A border alone is insufficient unless the candidate period tiles the full length.

frames.caption: For ababab, build the border lengths for every prefix.
The longest proper border is abab, length L=4.
The candidate block ab tiles all six characters exactly three times.
Contrast aba: its border length is 1, but candidate period 2 does not divide length 3.
frames.state: a nonempty border alone does not prove repetition

questions.title: Longest Happy Prefix
questions.prompt: Return the longest nonempty prefix that is also a proper suffix, or an empty string when none exists.
questions.why: Compute the prefix function once and return s[:pi[n−1]]. The table directly answers the longest-border question, including overlapping prefix and suffix occurrences.

frames.caption: At prefix aba, a is both prefix and suffix, giving pi[2]=1.
At prefix abab, ab is a border of length 2.
At the end, prefix abab equals suffix abab beginning at index 2. Overlap is allowed.
Return the first four characters. The full string is excluded by the proper-prefix definition.

topics.title: Merge sort and cross-half counting
topics.subtitle: Sort smaller ranges, then count relationships while merging.
topics.summary: Merge sort divides a contiguous range in two, recursively sorts each half, and merges them with two pointers. Sorted halves also let you count relationships between their elements in linear time. Each index pair belongs to one recursive split, so internal-half counts plus cross-half counts cover all pairs without duplication.
principles: Use half-open ranges [lo,hi); a range of length zero or one is already sorted.
Merge sorted halves by taking the smaller front value, then append either remaining tail. A reusable buffer avoids repeated allocation.
Preserve original indices when answers belong to original positions; sorting only the values loses that association.
For strict smaller-than counts, merge equal left values first so equal right values do not contribute.
Prove the pair-count condition separately from the merge comparison. Each level does O(n) work, giving O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary buffer space plus O(log n) recursion depth.

frames.caption: Split the contiguous input into [5,2] and [6,1]. Every original left index precedes every original right index.
Recursively sort the left half and count its single ordinary inversion: 5>2.
Sort the right half and count 6>1.
During merge, right value 1 precedes both remaining left values 2 and 5: two cross-half inversions.
Finish the merge as [1,2,5,6]. The original array has four ordinary inversions.

questions.title: Sort an Array
questions.prompt: Sort the integer array in ascending order without using a built-in sort, meeting O(n log n) time.
questions.why: Recursively sort each contiguous half, merge through a shared buffer, then copy the merged range back. Merge sort gives a predictable O(n log n) bound with O(n) auxiliary space; discuss heapsort if the interviewer requires constant auxiliary space.

frames.caption: Split into [5,2] and [3,1], then recurse down to single elements.
Merge the left singleton ranges by selecting 2 before 5.
Merge the right singleton ranges by selecting 1 before 3.
Merge [2,5] with [1,3]: take 1,2,3, then the remaining 5.

questions.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
questions.prompt: For each original position, count values strictly smaller than it to its right.
questions.why: Merge (value, original_index) pairs. Whenever a right value is emitted before a left value, increment a moved-right counter. Add that counter when emitting each left value. Equal values take from the left first. Recursive internal counts and cross-half counts accumulate at original indices.

frames.caption: Sorting [5,2] adds one to the answer for original index 0.
Sorting [6,1] adds one to the answer for original index 2.
Merge sorted halves [2,5] and [1,6]. Emit 1, then 2; one right-side value is smaller than 2.
Emit 5 with moved-right count 1, adding its cross-half smaller value.

questions.title: Reverse Pairs
questions.prompt: Count original index pairs i<j for which nums[i] is greater than twice nums[j].
questions.why: After sorting both halves, scan left values in ascending order and advance a right pointer while left>2*right. Add how many right values qualify for each left value, then perform a normal merge. The counting pointer never retreats. Python integers avoid overflow; fixed-width languages need a wider type for doubling.

frames.caption: Split at index 2: left [2,4] and right [3,5,1]. Count internal pairs recursively.
The sorted halves are [2,4] and [1,3,5]. Count cross pairs before the final normal merge.
For left value 4, only right value 1 qualifies. The next value 3 fails because 4≤6.
Add internal and cross counts, then merge the sorted ranges.

topics.title: Fenwick tree and dynamic prefix sums
topics.subtitle: Update a point and query a prefix in logarithmic time.
topics.summary: A Fenwick tree stores overlapping power-of-two blocks of an array. In its one-based internal representation, tree[i] covers lowbit(i)=i&−i elements ending at i. A prefix query jumps left with i-=lowbit(i); a point addition updates every covering block with i+=lowbit(i). This supports changing sums or frequency counts in O(log n) per operation.
principles: Convert external zero-based positions to one-based internal indices; index zero is only a stopping sentinel, never an update position.
prefix(i) sums internal positions 1 through i. An external inclusive range [l,r] is prefix(r+1)−prefix(l).
For assignment, compute delta=new−old and add delta to all covering tree blocks; keep the old values separately.
A frequency tree can count values below a coordinate. Compress arbitrary values into sorted ranks while preserving equality.

Each operation visits O(log n) blocks using O(n) storage. The subtraction trick requires an invertible aggregate such as sum; this basic structure does not directly support arbitrary range minimum with arbitrary point replacements.

frames.caption: Displayed numbers are internal indices. Node 6 covers [5,6], while node 4 covers [1,4].
To query prefix 6, take tree[6], covering positions 5 and 6.
Next take tree[4], covering 1 through 4, then stop at zero. The blocks are disjoint.
To add delta at position 5, update nodes 5,6,8: each stored block includes position 5.
Queries decompose a prefix; updates repair its containing blocks. Neither scans all array elements.
frames.state: O(log n) per add or prefix query

questions.title: Range Sum Query - Mutable
questions.prompt: Support point assignments and inclusive range-sum queries on a changing array.
questions.why: Initialize a Fenwick tree from the array, retain the current values, and translate update(index,val) into add(index+1,val−old). Compute sumRange(l,r) as prefix(r+1)−prefix(l). Building by repeated adds takes O(n log n); each subsequent operation takes O(log n).

frames.caption: Initial values are [1,3,5]. The one-based tree stores [1,4,5] at nodes 1–3.
Assign external index 1 the value 2. This is an addition of −1 at internal position 2.
Update tree[2] from 4 to 3; the next ancestor is 4, outside this three-element tree.
prefix(3) takes tree[3]+tree[2], totaling 5+3.

questions.title: Create Sorted Array through Instructions
questions.prompt: Insert values in order and sum the smaller of the counts strictly below and strictly above each inserted value, modulo 1,000,000,007.
questions.why: Maintain frequencies by value or compressed rank. Before inserting x, less=prefix(rank−1) and greater=inserted_count−prefix(rank), excluding equals from both sides. Add min(less,greater), then increment x’s frequency.

frames.caption: Insert 1 into an empty frequency tree. Both strict-side counts are zero.
For 5 there is one smaller and no greater value. Insert 5 after querying.
For 6 there are two smaller and no greater values.
For 2, only 1 is smaller while 5 and 6 are greater.

questions.title: Queries on a Permutation With Key
questions.prompt: For each requested value, return its current zero-based position in the permutation and move it to the front.
questions.why: Reserve q empty positions before the initial m values. Store occupancy 1 for each value’s current position. Its current rank is prefix(position−1). Remove its old occupancy and place it in the next unused front slot. This avoids physically shifting the permutation and costs O((m+q) log(m+q)); a simple list also suffices for the original small constraints.

frames.caption: With queries [3,1,2,1], reserve four front slots. Initial values occupy internal positions 5–9. Query 3 at position 7.
Move 3 to slot 4. Value 1 at slot 5 now has one occupied slot before it.
frames.state: query 1 → rank=1 · move it to slot 3

frames.caption: Value 2 remains at slot 6. Slots 3 and 4 are occupied before it.
frames.state: query 2 → rank=2 · move it to slot 2

topics.title: Sweep line and boundary events
topics.subtitle: Process changes at boundaries instead of revisiting every interval.
topics.summary: A sweep line turns intervals into start and end events, sorts the event coordinates, and maintains the state between consecutive boundaries. Additive state needs only net deltas; an active maximum needs a heap or ordered multiset. Group events at the same coordinate before reporting the new state so touching intervals are handled consistently.
principles: Choose interval semantics first: [l,r) stops at r, while an inclusive integer range [l,r] can be represented by removal at r+1.
For sums or occupancy, add weight at the start and subtract it at the end; a running total reconstructs the active load.
Group all events at a coordinate before evaluating the state immediately to its right; avoid spurious intermediate changes.
For a skyline, track active heights with multiplicities or a heap with expiry. Removing one building must not remove another building of the same height.
With sparse coordinates, sort O(n) boundaries for O(n log n) processing. A dense bounded coordinate range may use a difference array and a linear scan.

frames.caption: Two half-open weighted intervals are [1,5) with weight 2 and [3,7) with weight 3. Only the four boundaries change the load.
At coordinate 1 the load becomes 2 and remains 2 until coordinate 3.
At coordinate 3 add 3; the intervals now overlap.
At coordinate 5 remove 2, leaving only the second interval.
At coordinate 7 remove 3. The sweep is complete without inspecting interior coordinates.

questions.title: Car Pooling
questions.prompt: Decide whether a vehicle can serve every trip without exceeding its capacity, dropping passengers before picking up new ones at the same location.
questions.why: Create +passengers at pickup and −passengers at dropoff. Aggregate deltas by location, sweep in ascending order, and reject if the resulting occupancy exceeds capacity. Half-open trips allow seats freed at a stop to be reused there.

frames.caption: Trips [2,1,5] and [3,3,7] begin with two passengers at location 1.
At location 3, three more passengers board.
For capacity 5, the same trips are possible. Two passengers leave at location 5.
The final three leave at location 7. Aggregating a drop and pickup at one stop avoids a false overflow.

questions.title: Corporate Flight Bookings
questions.prompt: Return the total reserved seats on each flight after bookings that add seats across inclusive flight-number ranges.
questions.why: For a booking [first,last,seats], add seats at first and subtract at last+1. Prefix-sum the differences for flights 1 through n. This performs every range addition in constant time, then reconstructs the final totals in O(n+bookings) time.

frames.caption: Booking [1,2,10] contributes +10 at flight 1 and −10 at flight 3.
Booking [2,3,20] contributes +20 at flight 2 and −20 at flight 4.
Booking [2,5,25] adds 25 at flight 2; its removal is at sentinel flight 6.
Prefix-sum only the real flights, excluding the sentinel.

questions.title: The Skyline Problem
questions.prompt: Return the key points where the maximum active building height changes.
questions.why: Sweep all unique starts and ends. At x, push buildings starting there into a max-heap of (height,end), then pop top entries with end≤x until the top is live. The heap top is the visible height, or zero. Emit one point only when this height changes. Expired buried entries can wait until they reach the top.

frames.caption: Buildings are [2,9,10], [3,7,15], [5,12,12]. At x=2 the active maximum is 10.
At x=3, height 15 hides height 10. The building starting at 5 has height 12 and changes no visible height.
At x=7, the height-15 building expires, exposing height 12.
At x=9 height 10 expires while hidden; at x=12 the last building ends.

topics.title: Dynamic programming on trees
topics.subtitle: Return a compact subtree summary and combine children after visiting them.
topics.summary: Tree DP uses postorder traversal to compute each node’s state from its children. Define precisely what a parent may receive: a height, one extendable path, or a pair of constrained choices. A complete answer inside the subtree may differ from the state returned upward. Because a tree has no shared descendant subproblems, a well-defined bottom-up recurrence visits each node once.
principles: Write the returned-state contract before the recurrence. It must contain exactly what the parent needs.
Compute children first, then combine their states; define the empty-subtree base case explicitly.
Separate a path that may extend to the parent from a complete path that can join both children.
When parent decisions constrain children, return one state per constraint, such as take and skip.
With constant-size states, time is O(n). Recursive traversal uses O(h) stack; a skewed Python tree may need an explicit postorder stack to avoid recursion-depth limits.

frames.caption: Tree edges are 1→2, 1→3, 2→4, 2→5. For a height summary, an empty subtree has height 0.
Node 2 receives both leaf heights and returns a single extendable height.
Node 3 is also a leaf, so its returned height is 1.
Root 1 receives heights 2 and 1. It can return height 3, while the complete path through it has 3 edges.
The parent summary and full answer measure different things. State that distinction to avoid off-by-one or branching errors.
frames.state: one subtree summary per node · O(n) work

questions.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
questions.prompt: Return the largest number of edges on a path between any two nodes; the path need not pass through the root.
questions.why: Return subtree height in nodes, using 0 for empty. At each node, left_height+right_height is a complete path length in edges; update the best diameter and return 1+max(left_height,right_height). A leaf contributes diameter 0.

frames.caption: For tree [1,2,3,4,5], nodes 4 and 5 return height 1.
At node 2, joining its child branches gives path 4→2→5.
At node 1, left height is 2 and right height is 1.
One longest path is 4→2→1→3; count edges rather than nodes.

steps: The leaves 3, 4, and 5 return height 1.
Node 2 can join the branches ending at 4 and 5, making a path of two edges. Its own returned height is 2.
The root receives heights 2 and 1. Joining them makes a three-edge path, such as 4 → 2 → 1 → 3.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: Every path reaches a highest node. Considering both branches at every node eventually considers that highest point of the longest path.
walkthrough.cost: O(n) time. Recursive stack space is O(h), where h is the height.
walkthrough.pitfall: Measure the returned height in nodes and the diameter in edges. A tree with one node has diameter 0.

questions.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
questions.prompt: Find the maximum sum of a nonempty simple path anywhere in a binary tree.
questions.why: Return node.val+max(0,left_gain,right_gain) as one extendable branch. Update a global best with node.val+max(0,left_gain)+max(0,right_gain), which can join both children locally. Initialize the best to negative infinity so all-negative trees still select one node.

frames.caption: Tree edges are −10→9, −10→20, 20→15, 20→7. Leaves return their own positive values.
At node 20, joining both children yields a complete path, but only one branch may be returned upward.
At −10, the complete candidate is −10+9+35=34, below the existing best.
The best path stays entirely in the right subtree. If all values were negative, keep the least-negative node.

steps: Leaves 15 and 7 return their own values. Node 20 can join them into a complete path worth 42.
Only one branch can continue upward from 20, so return 20 + 15 = 35.
At the root, the best joined path there is -10 + 9 + 35 = 34. Keep 42 as the overall best.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: A simple path can join at most two child branches at its highest node. A branch passed to the parent can extend into at most one child.
walkthrough.cost: O(n) time and O(h) recursive stack space.
walkthrough.pitfall: An all-negative tree still needs a nonempty path. Start the overall best at negative infinity or at the root’s value.

questions.title: House Robber III
questions.prompt: Choose tree nodes with maximum total value while never choosing a node and its direct child together.
questions.why: Return (take,skip). Taking a node forces both children to be skipped: take=value+left.skip+right.skip. Skipping it allows either state independently in each child: skip=max(left)+max(right). Return max(root.take,root.skip); this avoids recomputing grandchildren.

frames.caption: The root has children 2 and 3; their single children are 3 and 1. Leaves return their take/skip choices.
At node 2, taking yields 2; skipping allows its child 3.
At right child 3, taking yields 3; skipping yields 1.
Taking root gives 3+3+1=7. Skipping root gives max(2,3)+max(3,1)=6.

steps: Return two scores at each node, one for taking it and one for skipping it. The two lowest leaves return (3, 0) and (1, 0).
The left child returns (2, 3) and the right child returns (3, 1). Taking a parent requires skipping that parent’s child.
Taking the root gives 3 + 3 + 1 = 7. Skipping it lets each side choose its better score, giving 3 + 3 = 6.
walkthrough.whyItWorks: Once the current node’s choice is fixed, the child subtrees have no edges between them, so their best allowed scores can be added independently.
walkthrough.cost: O(n) time and O(h) recursive stack space.
walkthrough.pitfall: When skipping a node, either take or skip each child. Do not automatically take both children.

lesson.intuition: Picture a family tree. If you want to know how far the lowest descendant is, each child can answer for their own branch first. Once both answers are ready, you can answer for the parent. Tree dynamic programming uses the same idea. Each branch sends up a small summary, and the parent uses those summaries to solve its larger part of the problem.

terms.definition: A node with all of its descendants. Children are the nodes immediately below it.
Visit both children before doing the work at their parent.
The specific information a node reports to its parent, such as one height or two possible scores.

steps: Write down what an empty branch returns. For height measured in nodes, the answer is zero.
At a node, ask each child for its branch height.
Return one plus the larger height. The extra one counts the current node.
If you need the longest path anywhere, also check the path that joins both child branches at this node. Save that result separately because the parent can continue only one branch.

check.question: The left branch has height 2 and the right has height 1. How many edges are on the path that joins them through their parent?
check.answer: Three. Height 2 means two edges from the parent down the left side, and height 1 means one edge from the parent down the right.
